english: I missed you; I wanted to see you
use: Said on meeting a friend, partner or family member after time apart; the usual answer is 'watashi mo!' (me too).

example.romaji: Hisashiburi! Zutto aitakatta yo.
example.ja: 久しぶり！ずっと会いたかったよ。
example.english: Long time no see! I've really missed you.

examplePolite.ja: お久しぶりです。会いたかったです。
examplePolite.english: It's been a while. I've been wanting to see you.

notes: Japanese has no direct 'I miss you': past aitakatta covers the reunion, while 'aitai' (I want to see you) is for while you're still apart.

use: A bright, playful hello to a close friend, often with a wave across a room or at the start of a call or message.

example.romaji: Yahhoo! Gomen ne, chotto okureta.
example.ja: やっほー！ごめんね、ちょっと遅れた。
example.english: Hiya! Sorry, I'm a bit late.

notes: Sounds cheerful and a little cute; more common from women and young people. Also the shout people give from a mountaintop.

kana: れんらくしなくてごめん
politeJa: 連絡しなくてすみません
english: sorry I haven't been in touch
use: Opens a message or meeting with a friend you've gone quiet on; they'll usually brush it off with 'ii yo, ii yo'.

example.romaji: Zutto renraku shinakute gomen ne. Genki datta?
example.ja: ずっと連絡しなくてごめんね。元気だった？
example.english: Sorry I haven't been in touch for so long. How've you been?

examplePolite.romaji: Nagai aida renraku shinakute sumimasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: 長い間連絡しなくてすみませんでした。
examplePolite.english: I'm sorry I haven't been in touch for so long.

notes: With people you should be formal with, the set phrase is 'gobusata shite imasu'.

use: Asked before an invitation, with the day first: 'doyoubi aiteru?'. Answer 'aiteru yo' or 'gomen, chotto...'.

example.romaji: Doyoubi no yoru, aiteru?
example.ja: 土曜日の夜、空いてる？
example.english: Are you free Saturday night?

examplePolite.romaji: Raishuu no getsuyoubi wa aite imasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 来週の月曜日は空いていますか？

notes: Also used for seats and rooms: 'kono seki aite imasu ka?' is 'is this seat free?'.

use: Invites someone to join something you're already going to do; 'iku iku!' is the eager yes.

example.romaji: Ima kara konbini iku kedo, issho ni kuru?
example.ja: 今からコンビニ行くけど、一緒に来る？
example.english: I'm heading to the convenience store. Want to come along?

examplePolite.romaji: Kore kara shokuji ni ikimasu kedo, issho ni kimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: これから食事に行きますけど、一緒に来ますか？
examplePolite.english: We're going to eat now. Would you like to come along?

notes: Use kuru when you're going and they join you; 'issho ni ikanai?' (shall we go together?) when it's a joint plan.

use: A soft lead-in to an invitation, usually with a time; answer 'betsu ni nai yo' (not really) if you're free.

example.romaji: Kondo no nichiyoubi, nanika yotei aru?
example.ja: 今度の日曜日、何か予定ある？
example.english: Got any plans this Sunday?

examplePolite.romaji: Kyou no yoru wa nanika yotei arimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今日の夜は何か予定ありますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you have any plans tonight?

use: Invites a friend to your place; uchi here means 'my home', and dropping ni is normal in speech.

example.romaji: Atarashii geemu katta n da. Uchi kuru?
example.ja: 新しいゲーム買ったんだ。うち来る？
example.english: I bought a new game. Want to come over?

examplePolite.romaji: Yokattara, kondo uchi ni kimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: よかったら、今度うちに来ませんか？
examplePolite.english: If you'd like, why not come over sometime?

notes: Uchi can also mean 'our family' or 'our company', depending on context.

english: I'll fit around you; whatever suits you
use: Your answer when someone asks when or where to meet, handing them the choice.

example.romaji: Itsu demo ii yo. Sotchi ni awaseru yo.
example.ja: いつでもいいよ。そっちに合わせるよ。
example.english: Any time's fine. I'll fit around you.

examplePolite.romaji: Watashi wa itsu demo daijoubu desu. Awasemasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 私はいつでも大丈夫です。合わせますよ。
examplePolite.english: Any time works for me. I'll fit around you.

notes: Literally 'I'll match (you)'. The polite version is often 'sochira ni awasemasu'.

use: Closes the planning once everyone agrees on a time or place; often 'jaa, kimari ne!'.

example.romaji: Jaa, doyoubi no juuniji ni eki de. Kimari!
example.ja: じゃあ、土曜日の12時に駅で。決まり！
example.english: So, noon Saturday at the station. It's a deal!

notes: From kimaru (to be decided); 'mou kimatteru' means it's already settled.

use: Seals a plan or favour so the other person can't back out; they answer 'un, yakusoku'.

example.romaji: Kondo wa zettai kite ne. Yakusoku ne.
example.ja: 今度は絶対来てね。約束ね。
example.english: You'd better come next time. Promise?

examplePolite.romaji: Kondo wa zettai kite kudasai ne. Yakusoku desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 今度は絶対来てくださいね。約束ですよ。
examplePolite.english: Please make sure you come next time. It's a promise.

notes: Yakusoku suru is 'to promise'; 'yakusoku ga aru' means 'I have plans with someone'.

english: I'll come along; I'll keep you company
use: Offers to join someone for something they need or want to do: shopping, a drink, waiting.

example.romaji: Kaimono? Ii yo, tsukiau yo.
example.ja: 買い物？いいよ、付き合うよ。
example.english: Shopping? Sure, I'll come with you.

examplePolite.romaji: Yokereba, saigo made otsukiai shimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: よければ、最後までお付き合いしますよ。
examplePolite.english: If you like, I'll keep you company to the end.

notes: With a person, 'X to tsukiau' means 'to date X', and 'tsukiatte kudasai' can be a love confession, so watch the context.

english: yeah, I can make it; sure, easy
use: A quick, upbeat yes when asked if you can make it, or encouragement that something is doable.

example.romaji: Shichiji? Ikeru ikeru, daijoubu.
example.ja: 7時？行ける行ける、大丈夫。
example.english: Seven? Yeah, I can make it, no problem.

notes: Also said about food or a challenge: 'kore ikeru' is 'this is pretty good' or 'I can do this'.

use: Jumps on board with a plan or idea someone just pitched; sounds keen and a bit playful.

example.romaji: Onsen ryokou? Sono hanashi, notta!
example.ja: 温泉旅行？その話、乗った！
example.english: A hot spring trip? Count me in!

notes: From noru (to get on board). Just 'notta!' works too.

use: Softens a no: you can't make it this time but want to be asked again. Also said when you hear about a fun outing you missed.

example.romaji: Kyou wa muri da kedo, mata kondo sasotte.
example.ja: 今日は無理だけど、また今度誘って。
example.english: I can't today, but invite me next time.

examplePolite.romaji: Zannen desu. Mata kondo sasotte kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 残念です。また今度誘ってください。
examplePolite.english: That's a shame. Please invite me next time.

notes: Sasou is 'to invite'; 'sasotte kurete arigatou' is 'thanks for inviting me'.

use: A light, friendly way to skip an outing without a long excuse; fine with friends, too blunt with a boss.

example.romaji: Gomen, tsukareteru kara kyou wa pasu.
example.ja: ごめん、疲れてるから今日はパス。
example.english: Sorry, I'm tired, so I'll pass today.

notes: Pasu works for anything you skip: food, a turn in a game, a question you won't answer.

use: The standard soft refusal: say it and trail off, and the other person understands it's a no.

example.romaji: Ikitai kedo, ashita hayai n da yo ne.
example.ja: 行きたいけど、明日早いんだよね。
example.english: I'd love to, but I've got an early start tomorrow.

examplePolite.romaji: Ikitai n desu kedo, sono hi wa chotto...
examplePolite.ja: 行きたいんですけど、その日はちょっと…
examplePolite.english: I'd love to, but that day's a bit...

notes: Leaving the sentence hanging is the polite part; you don't have to spell out the reason.

use: A non-committal maybe about going or doing something; it can work as a polite no.

example.romaji: Ki ga muitara iku kamo.
example.ja: 気が向いたら行くかも。
example.english: I might go if I feel like it.

examplePolite.romaji: Ki ga muitara, zehi asobi ni kite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 気が向いたら、ぜひ遊びに来てください。
examplePolite.english: Do drop by whenever you feel like it.

notes: Ki ga muku = to feel inclined. Also an easygoing invite: 'ki ga muitara kite ne' (come if you feel like it).

politeJa: 今日はありがとうございました
use: Said when parting after time together, and often again by text that night; reply 'kochira koso' (likewise).

example.romaji: Kyou wa arigatou. Sugoku tanoshikatta.
example.ja: 今日はありがとう。すごく楽しかった。
example.english: Thanks for today. I had a great time.

examplePolite.romaji: Kyou wa hontou ni arigatou gozaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は本当にありがとうございました。
examplePolite.english: Thank you so much for today.

notes: The polite form uses past gozaimashita because the event is over.

english: I'll walk you home; I'll drive you
use: Offers to see someone home or to the station at the end of the night; the polite refusal is 'ii yo, daijoubu'.

example.romaji: Mou osoi kara, eki made okuru yo.
example.ja: もう遅いから、駅まで送るよ。
example.english: It's late, so I'll walk you to the station.

examplePolite.romaji: Kuruma de ie made okurimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 車で家まで送りますよ。

notes: Okuru also means 'to send': 'shashin okuru ne' is 'I'll send you the photos'.

politeJa: 着いたらLINEしてください
english: text me when you get home
use: Said when parting at night so you know they got home safe; answer 'un, suru ne'.

example.romaji: Ki o tsukete ne. Tsuitara rain shite.
example.ja: 気をつけてね。着いたらLINEして。
example.english: Get home safe. Text me when you're back.

examplePolite.romaji: Otsukaresama deshita. Tsuitara rain shite kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: お疲れさまでした。着いたらLINEしてくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Thanks for today. Please message me when you get home.

notes: LINE is Japan's main messaging app, so 'rain suru' means 'to text'; 'renraku shite' (get in touch) works for any app.
